title: Harvesting and storing onions
subtitle: Lifting, ripening down, drying, and storing for months
excerpt: Onions are lifted in July and August when the foliage has yellowed and fallen naturally. They need two to four weeks of drying in a warm, airy place before storage. Well-dried onions store for three to six months in a cool, well-ventilated spot.
sourceNotes: RHS onion growing guide (rhs.org.uk). Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), kitchen garden section. Mrs Loudon, The Lady's Country Companion (1845), Project Gutenberg.

glossaryTerms.definition: The process of allowing the neck of a harvested onion to dry completely before storage. The neck is the constricted area between the bulb and the dried foliage. A fully dry neck is thin, papery, and firm; a damp or thick neck indicates incomplete drying and the bulb will rot within weeks of storage. Check the neck by pressing firmly with a thumb before storing; any give means more drying is needed.

content.text: Onions are ready to lift when most of the foliage has fallen over and turned yellow or brown. This happens naturally in July and August without any forcing. The period after lifting is as important as the growing: onions that are not dried thoroughly before storage will rot.

Wait until approximately two thirds of the foliage has naturally fallen. Do not force it over by hand; a traditional recommendation that is now known to allow rot to enter through the broken neck. Lift on a dry day. Loosen the soil with a fork first to avoid tearing the roots; undamaged roots slow down the drying process less. Lift carefully and inspect each bulb; set aside any with soft spots, cuts, or thick necks to use fresh first.

If dry weather is forecast, leave bulbs on the soil surface in full sun for several days; this starts the drying quickly. Turn them once or twice. Bring under cover at night or before rain; wet bulbs in contact with cold soil resume root activity and slow down curing.

Move to a greenhouse, cold frame, shed, or well-ventilated porch for the main drying period. Lay in a single layer on wire racks, slatted shelving, or old window frames raised off the ground. Good airflow is essential; cramped damp conditions cause mould on the outer skins. Check the
after two weeks; only move to long-term storage when the neck is completely dry and hard.

Store in nets, old tights, or plaited ropes in a cool (5 to 10°C), dry, well-ventilated space. A cool shed, garage, or larder is better than a warm kitchen. Check monthly and remove any starting to soften. Well-dried bulbs from a late-sown variety (Bedfordshire Champion, Sturon) store until December to February; early varieties store less well.
